comparison: Strong agreement on neural discrimination of OSR from sucrose (C34-C45). Both recognize the sophisticated electrophysiological methodology and clustering analysis. Peer review also includes behavioral claims C46-C48, acknowledging the disconnect between neural discrimination and behavioral response.

OpenEval addresses behavioral findings C46-C49 showing no behavioral discrimination despite neural differences. Peer review includes these claims (C46-C48) as part of their broader evaluation, accepting the neural-behavioral disconnect as compelling evidence.

Strong agreement on quinine as effective positive control (C50-C60). Both evaluations accept the dose-dependent neural and behavioral effects. Peer review additionally includes mechanistic claims C89-C90 and post-ingestive feedback claims C97-C100, treating quinine data as methodologically sound validation.

Strong agreement that field-realistic pesticide concentrations produce no detectable neural effects (C61-C62, C91). Both evaluations support the conclusion that bees cannot taste neonicotinoids with mouthparts. Peer review groups these with broader conclusions C5-C6, C8, C81, C88 about overall inability to detect pesticides.

Strong agreement on extreme concentration effects (C63-C73). Both accept that only toxicologically irrelevant concentrations produce neural effects insufficient for computational discrimination. Peer review includes these with broader mechanistic claims C7, C85-C87, C92-C93 about population coding and detection thresholds.

Strong agreement on behavioral data showing no avoidance (C74-C80). Both accept that bees consume lethal doses without detection. Peer review also includes claims C84, C103, C105 about consumption relative to LD50, treating the complete absence of avoidance as compelling and central to study significance.

Partial overlap on behavioral claims C74-C77. Both evaluations support the absence of avoidance behavior. Peer review groups these with broader conclusions about inability to detect field-realistic doses (C5-C6, C61-C62, C81, C88, C91).

Strong agreement on primary conclusions (C5-C8, C81-C88). Both evaluations find these well-supported by comprehensive electrophysiological and behavioral data. Peer review explicitly states results 'strongly suggest' bees cannot perceive field-realistic pesticide doses and describes conclusions as 'sound.'

Agreement on quinine mechanistic findings (C89-C90) showing effects on firing rates but not burst structure. OpenEval explicitly evaluates these claims; peer review implicitly accepts them as part of the methodologically sound quinine positive control data.

Agreement on population coding mechanism (C92-C96, C94-C96 overlap). Both accept the correlation between clustering and behavior. OpenEval notes C96 is somewhat speculative; peer review praises the sophisticated methodology, implicitly accepting mechanistic interpretations about population coding.

Partial overlap on mechanistic integration claims C92-C93. Both evaluations support the interpretation linking electrophysiology, computation, and behavior. Peer review groups these with broader findings about insufficient neural effects for detection.

Agreement on post-ingestive feedback interpretation (C97-C100). OpenEval finds the inference reasonable given behavioral patterns; peer review does not challenge these claims, treating them as part of the methodologically sound quinine control data.

Partial overlap on toxicological context claims C103, C105 about pesticide consumption relative to LD50. Both evaluations accept these calculations. Peer review emphasizes that bees consuming lethal doses is central to study significance.

Strong agreement on population coding mechanism (C106-C110). OpenEval finds this well-supported by clustering analyses; peer review praises the sophisticated methodology and combination of approaches, implicitly accepting the mechanistic interpretations.

Partial agreement with uncertainty on reconciliation with previous literature (C111-C117). OpenEval finds the interpretation logical and well-cited; peer review finds the reconciliation incomplete, requesting expanded discussion for wider context, though acknowledging authors addressed concerns about being combative.

Partial agreement with uncertainty on methodological critique of previous work (C118-C121). OpenEval finds the critique valid but notes speculation for bumblebees; peer review requests broader context, suggesting the reconciliation with conflicting studies needs expansion.

Agreement with uncertainty on ecological predictions (C9-C10, C122-C127). OpenEval finds the logic sound but notes C10 is speculative and untested in field conditions; peer review requests broader ecological context, indicating this framing requires strengthening though not explicitly challenging the claims.

OpenEval evaluates background context claims C1-C3, C11-C15 about bee ecology and pesticide impacts as well-supported by appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these introductory framing claims.

OpenEval evaluates literature characterization claims C4, C16-C19 about contradictory findings and knowledge gaps as appropriately supported. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though peer review notes study was motivated by conflicting results.

OpenEval evaluates methodological background claims C20-C33 about mechanistic framework and experimental rationale as well-supported by appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these technical background claims.
